agent_notes: The Hebrew verse 1 carries the superscription (words 1-2, KJV 143:0) and the first line of the prayer (KJV 143:1). Both are glossed and translated here as one verse. LXX adds 'when his son pursued him', which is not in the Hebrew and is not used.

בארץ מישור: 'land of level ground' (KJV 'land of uprightness'). Ibn Ezra offers an alternative reading with an implied ב on רוחך ('by your good spirit lead me'); I kept the Masoretic division, in which 'your spirit is good' is a clause of its own, as the accents mark it.
Metzudat David's comment on the second half is cut off in Malbim's text in the packet ('אמר' with nothing after it); I did not rely on it.

תצמית / והאבדת are future-form with perfect-with-waw: the English versions (YLT) read them as statement; KJV/ASV as wish. Context of imperatives in vv. 7-11 supports a wish ('may you cut off'), which is how the dramatic layer renders it, while the literal layer keeps the plain future.
אֶת in 'את־עבדך' is the preposition 'with' (as Ibn Ezra reads it), not the object marker; STEPBible has it right, so I glossed it 'with'. The sense is 'do not enter into judgment with your servant'.

agent_notes: תתעטף: KJV/ASV 'overwhelmed' and YLT 'feeble' are the usual Hithpael of עטף 'to wrap, to be faint'. Literal layer keeps the wrapping image ('wraps itself over me'); the five versions agree on the sense, not on the image.

Reviewer request applied: the sentence about the KJV flattening the second and third verbs is removed. The KJV note now says only that all three verbs are in the present, where the Hebrew has two perfects and a closing imperfect.

The two perfects (zakharti, hagiti) are rendered 'I have remembered', 'I have meditated' in the literal layer; the closing imperfect asoḥeaḥ is 'I muse'. STEPBible glosses the last as 'I meditate'; I kept 'muse' so that hagiti and asoḥeaḥ stay two different words in English, as they are in Hebrew.

agent_notes: נפשי glossed 'my throat/self' in the literal layer note only; in the line 'like a land exhausted for you' the thirst sense comes from the simile, not from the word. KJV 'thirsteth' is an interpretive addition; Hebrew has עיפה 'faint, weary'.

Reviewer request applied: zu is read as the poetic relative 'which', following STEPBible and Metzudat David (הדרך אשר אלך בה). The earlier claim that the phrase means 'a road he is already on', and that the KJV is less exact, is dropped.

Gloss of nasati nafshi: STEPBible has 'desire my' for nafshi; I kept 'my soul' because the idiom 'lift up the nefesh' is the same in the KJV and the other versions. Ibn Ezra and Meiri tie it to Deut 24:15 (hope), Meiri also to prayer (Lam 3:41).

agent_notes: אליך כסיתי is a famous crux. The Hebrew says literally 'to you I have covered'. Ancient and medieval readings differ: 'I have hidden [my troubles] from others, to you' (Rashi, Radak, Malbim), 'I have taken cover with you' (a reading behind KJV/ASV 'flee to thee to hide me', assuming כסה = חסה), or the Targum's 'your word I have appointed as my redeemer'. The literal layer keeps the Hebrew; the dramatic layer follows the shelter reading, which most English versions take.

(PS.143.9 YLT: "Near Thee I am covered.")
